slides.0.title: Vallée de la Marne and Côte des Blancs
slides.0.subtitle: The valley of Meunier and the chalk slope of Chardonnay
slides.1.title: Vallée de la Marne: the valley of Meunier
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Along the river
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Vineyards run along both banks of the Marne towards Paris, mostly on steep hillsides (Comité Champagne)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Pinot Noir east, Meunier west
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Near Épernay in the east Pinot Noir dominates; moving west Meunier becomes dominant (Comité Champagne)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Why Meunier suits it
slides.1.highlights.2.content: A common explanation: Meunier buds later and copes better with spring frost and the damp valley, so it became the valley's workhorse
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Two Grand Crus
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Aÿ (written Ay in the INAO text) and Tours-sur-Marne
slides.1.content: The valley is Meunier's home, yet its eastern Grand Cru is still famous for Pinot Noir.
slides.2.title: Valley villages and pruning
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Aÿ and Tours-sur-Marne
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Aÿ is known for Pinot Noir (WineWithSeth); Tours-sur-Marne is the valley's other Grand Cru
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Premier Cru examples
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Valley villages on the specification list: Hautvillers, Cumières, Dizy, Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, Champillon, Avenay-Val-d’Or, Bisseuil and Mutigny
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The Vallée de la Marne pruning
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Written into the specification: this pruning is for Meunier only, with one courson (up to 3 buds), one baguette (up to 9 buds) and one prolongement (up to 6 buds), the fruiting cane tied no higher than 0.60 m above the ground
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Extending west
slides.2.highlights.3.content: The valley continues west into the Aisne, which holds about 10% of the vineyard area (figures differ by source; see Level 1)
slides.2.content: The valley has many Premier Crus on the list but only two Grand Crus.
slides.3.title: Côte des Blancs: the chalk slope of Chardonnay
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Landscape
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Named for Chardonnay, a chalk slope running north-east to south-west at right angles to the Marne valley and about 6 to 9 miles long (Comité Champagne)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Six Grand Crus
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Avize, Chouilly, Cramant, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Oger and Oiry (INAO specification)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Style tendencies
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Common descriptions: Cramant floral and delicate, Le Mesnil tight, mineral and long-lived, Avize precise and powerful, Oger rounder (descriptive, not rules, not tested)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Premier Cru and the southern neighbours
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Premier Cru examples: Vertus, Cuis, Grauves, Pierry and Bergères-lès-Vertus; the Côte de Sézanne further south and Montgueux west of Troyes are also mainly Chardonnay but are not part of the Côte des Blancs
slides.3.content: Chardonnay plus chalk equals the Côte des Blancs, the heartland of Blanc de Blancs.
slides.4.title: Check: Grand Cru and variety limits
slides.4.highlights.0.title: No variety limit in the current text
slides.4.highlights.0.content: The INAO specification puts all 17 villages in one clause with no variety-based restriction, including Chouilly, Tours-sur-Marne and Aÿ
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Traces of the old price scale
slides.4.highlights.1.content: The old scale priced by colour: Chouilly black grapes at 95% (white at 100%), Tours-sur-Marne white at 90% (black at 100%); Coligny and Étréchy ranked Premier Cru for white grapes only (compiled by champagneclub; the inference about 100% is ours)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Customary shorthand
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Chouilly leans Chardonnay, Tours-sur-Marne Pinot Noir and Aÿ is famous for Pinot Noir: style and custom, not current rules, and not tested
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Rules when labelling
slides.4.highlights.3.content: When Grand/Premier Cru or a village is named, all base-wine grapes must come from that village; naming a single variety requires 100% of that variety (type no taller than 3 mm and half the AOC name)
slides.4.content: Conclusion: teach these as tendencies and never present variety limits for Grand Cru villages as law.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
Moving west along the Vallée de la Marne, which variety becomes more dominant?
Comité Champagne: Pinot Noir dominates near Épernay in the east and Meunier takes over moving west.
How many Grand Cru villages does the Côte des Blancs have?
Avize, Chouilly, Cramant, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Oger and Oiry make six.
Which two villages are the Grand Crus of the Vallée de la Marne?
Hautvillers and Dizy are Premier Cru; Avize and Oger are in the Côte des Blancs; Bouzy and Verzenay are in the Montagne de Reims.
